procedural_history.impugned_order: Order dated 13th December 1954 issued by the Central Board of Revenue under s. 5(7-A) of the Income-Tax Act, transferring the petitioner's assessment records from Calcutta to the Income Tax Officer, Special Circle, Ranchi.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: No high court proceedings are mentioned in the text.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: Original Jurisdiction: Petition No. 271 of 1955. The petitioner filed an application under Art. 32 of the Constitution.

issue.issue_text: Whether an Act, being general and applicable to all persons and offences, cannot be said to discriminate, and that any charge of discrimination can only be levelled against the misuse of the Act by the executive authority.

law.fact_text: Article 14 of the Constitution forbids discrimination and can be violated by a law that is discriminatory in its substance or procedure.
law.label: law

law.fact_text: The presumption that a legislature understands the needs of its people and that its enactments are constitutional is of little help when a statute, on its face, contains no classification or guiding principles for its application.
law.label: law

application.fact_text: The Court considered the argument that if a law is general and applies to all persons and offenses, it cannot be discriminatory, and any discrimination must arise from the executive's misuse of the law.
application.label: application

application.fact_text: The Court rejected this argument, stating that accepting it would mean that Article 14 could be "easily defeated."
application.label: application

application.fact_text: The Court identified the "fallacy" in the argument, explaining that it overlooks the fact that "insidious discrimination" can be "incorporated in the Act itself."
application.label: application

application.fact_text: A law can be drafted in such a way that it enables or facilitates discrimination. In such cases, any discriminatory action taken by the executive would be "ultimately traceable to" the flawed Act.
application.label: application

reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the argument. It held that a law, even if it appears general, can be inherently discriminatory if it is drafted in a way that allows for arbitrary and discriminatory application. In such a scenario, the discrimination is not merely a result of executive misuse but is incorporated within the Act itself, making the Act unconstitutional.

arguments.issue_text: Whether an Act, being general and applicable to all persons and offences, cannot be said to discriminate, and that any charge of discrimination can only be levelled against the misuse of the Act by the executive authority.
appellant_arguments: The Act itself (specifically section 5(7-A) of the Income Tax Act) is unconstitutional and violates Article 14 of the Constitution, which guarantees equality before the law. The power granted by the Act is discriminatory in nature, not just its potential for misuse.
respondent_arguments: The Act is a general law applicable to all persons and offenses and therefore cannot be inherently discriminatory. Any discrimination that occurs is not due to the Act itself but results from its improper or malicious application (misuse) by the executive authority. Therefore, one cannot challenge the validity of the Act on grounds of discrimination, only the specific actions taken under it.

cases.principle: A law or order can be struck down if it confers unrestricted power on a single individual without any checks to ensure proper execution or prevent injustice.

cases.case_name: Unnamed case (judgment of Fazl Ali J.)
cases.principle: A law can be challenged for discrimination if the 'insidious discrimination complained of is incorporated in the Act itself', making any discriminatory action traceable back to the statute. This counters the argument that only the executive misuse of a law, not the law itself, can be challenged.

cases.case_name: others v. The State of Bihar
cases.principle: The presumption of a law's constitutionality is of little assistance when the statute on its face contains no classification and provides no basis for selecting individuals or groups for differential treatment.

cases.case_name: State of Madras v. V. G. Row
cases.principle: Cited for the same principle as the Coal Control Case (that laws conferring unrestricted power can be struck down), extending the principle from cases under Article 19 to the present case under Article 14.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: In order to pass the test of permissible classification, two conditions must be fulfilled: (1) the classification must be founded on an intelligible differentia which distinguishes persons or things that are grouped together from others left out of the group, and (2) the differentia must have a rational relation to the object sought to be achieved by the statute in question. Such selection or differentiation must not be arbitrary and must rest upon a rational basis, having regard to the object which the legislature has in view.
obiter: The presumption in favour of the constitutionality of a legislative enactment is of little or no assistance when, on the face of the statute, there is no classification at all.
Article 14 sets out an attitude of mind, a way of life, rather than a precise rule of law.
Decisions on the same point will vary as conditions vary; it is not the law that alters but the changing conditions of the times.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court rejects the argument that a general Act applicable to all cannot be discriminatory and that only its misuse by the executive can be challenged. The court reasons that when a statute confers unrestricted and arbitrary power on an executive authority to select individuals for differential treatment, without any guiding principles or basis for classification within the law itself, the Act itself is unconstitutional. The court has previously struck down the Act or Order itself when it confers such unrestricted power, not merely the executive action taken under it. The fact that an executive body, rather than Parliament, is exercising this arbitrary power does not make the situation constitutionally better.
legal_tests_applied: For a law to be constitutional under Article 14, it must pass a two-part test: (1) the classification must be founded on an intelligible differentia which distinguishes those that are grouped together from others, and (2) that differentia must have a rational relation to the object sought to be achieved by the Act.

When on the face of a statute there is no classification at all, and no attempt has been made to select any individual or group with reference to any differentiating attribute, the presumption of constitutionality is of little or no assistance.
policy_considerations: There is a significant difference between investing a judicial authority with powers of transfer and investing non-judicial bodies with such powers, because judges are bound to act in accordance with recognized procedures and the laws of natural justice. In this case, the power granted to the executive allows for peremptory orders with no hearing and no recorded reasons.

The Constitution was enacted for the benefit of the people, and granting unchecked power to transfer cases from one end of India to the other without warning or reason undermines the rights and convenience of the assessee, which the law had previously treated as a valuable right.
